candidates.attacker_control: An attacker who holds any valid FF4j web API credential — including an intentionally read-only user/apiKey created through `ApiConfig.createUser(name, password, true, false, null)` / `createApiKey(key, true, false, null)` whose permissions are only {READ} — controls the HTTP method/path/body sent to the API. Example targets: `POST /<context>/api/ff4j/store/clear`, `POST /<context>/api/ff4j/propertyStore/clear`, `POST /<context>/api/ff4j/store/createSchema` and `POST /<context>/api/ff4j/store/groups/{group}/enable|disable`.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: • If ApiConfig.isAutorize() is false, no authorization filter is registered at all — but that is the explicitly unsecured mode; the flaw applies exactly when the operator enables the documented authorization feature. • @PermitAll/@DenyAll are method-level only and do not apply to these endpoints. • Registering Jersey's own RolesAllowedDynamicFeature would enforce class-level annotations for methods lacking one, but the store resources declare class-level ROLE_READ, so a READ-only principal would still satisfy the fallback for /clear and /createSchema. • The filter also silently allows annotated methods when the request SecurityContext is not an FF4jSecurityContext (the `instanceof` guard at lines 82-98 falls through to `return`), which is a related fail-open facet, not a mitigation. • No source in the snapshot registers an additional role-checking mechanism (Jersey feature, servlet filter) for these paths.
candidates.impact: Privilege escalation from read-only API access to full write/admin-equivalent operations: deletion of all feature flags and all properties (configuration/integrity loss, which can silently re-enable or disable protected functionality), execution of schema DDL, cache flushes, and group-wide enable/disable of features. The read-only/write separation that ApiConfig and the `@RolesAllowed` annotations are meant to provide is ineffective.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) The web API is deployed in the intended secured mode, i.e. an ApiConfig subclass with `setAutorize(true)` so that FF4jApiApplicationJersey2x registers both FF4jAuthenticationFilter and FF4jAuthorizationFilter (lines 92-95 and 127-137). (2) The attacker possesses a valid credential accepted by FF4jAuthenticationFilter (HTTP Basic or apiKey); READ-only is sufficient. (3) No additional container/Jersey role enforcement (e.g. Jersey `RolesAllowedDynamicFeature` or servlet-level role constraints) is layered on top.
candidates.root_cause: In `FF4jAuthorizationFilter.filter()`, authorization is only evaluated when the *resource method* itself carries `@RolesAllowed` (`isRolesAllowed()` checks `info.getResourceMethod().getAnnotation(RolesAllowed.class)`); if the method has no method-level annotation the filter simply returns and the request is allowed, regardless of the class-level `@RolesAllowed`. Additionally, `getRoles()` unions the class-level and method-level role arrays and the decision is `allowed if the user holds ANY role in the union`, so a class-level `READ` satisfies a method-level `WRITE`. The store resources declare only class-level `@RolesAllowed(ROLE_READ)` while exposing destructive POST endpoints (`/clear`, `/createSchema`, cache clear) with no method-level `WRITE` annotation, and `GroupResource` declares class-level READ with method-level WRITE on enable/disable — in all these cases a READ-only principal is accepted.
candidates.title: Read-only API credentials can perform destructive/write operations because role enforcement ignores class-level @RolesAllowed and ORs class+method roles
candidates.trace:
1. FF4jApiApplicationJersey2x.init(): `apiConfig.isAutorize()` → `enableAuthenticationFilter()` and `enableAuthorizationFilter()` register both filters for the JAX-RS application.
2. Attacker sends `Authorization: Basic base64(user:pass)` for a read-only user and `POST .../ff4j/store/clear`.
3. FF4jAuthenticationFilter validates the credential (`apiConfig.getUsers().get(lap[0])` + password compare) and builds `new FF4jSecurityContext(user, BASIC, permissionSet)` where permissionSet is {READ}; it stores it as the request SecurityContext.
4. FF4jAuthorizationFilter.filter() runs: `isDenyAll()` false, `isPermitAll()` false, `isRolesAllowed()` is false because `FeatureStoreResource.clearFeatures()` has no method-level `@RolesAllowed` → the role-check block is skipped and the method returns, authorizing the request.
5. Jersey invokes `FeatureStoreResource.clearFeatures()` → `getFeatureStore().clear()`, which empties the entire feature store (`FeatureStore.clear()` documented as "Empty features set", implemented e.g. InMemoryFeatureStore/AbstractFeatureStore).
6. The same pattern reaches `PropertyStoreResource.clearProperties()`, both `createSchema()` endpoints (DB DDL), the cache-clear POSTs, and (through the union in `getRoles()`) `GroupResource.operationEnable/operationDisable`: class-level {READ} ∪ method-level {WRITE} = {READ, WRITE}, so the READ-only principal matches.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation was not possible (no execution): the exact filter ordering relative to FF4jAuthenticationFilter, and the absence of externally configured role enforcement in any particular deployment, are assumptions. The conclusion that class-level annotations are bypassed is based on reading `FF4jAuthorizationFilter.isRolesAllowed()/filter()/getRoles()` only; a deployment that registers extra security would change the exploitability but not the flawed code.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper authorization / privilege escalation (CWE-863; also CWE-862, CWE-602-adjacent)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the 580-file multi-module snapshot (ff4j-core, ff4j-web, ff4j-webapi, ff4j-webapi-jersey2x, ff4j-security-spring/shiro, ff4j-config-properties/yaml, ff4j-aop, ff4j-jmx, ff4j-cli, ff4j-utils-json, ff4j-strategy-drools and the ~25 store modules). Deep review focused on the web/API trust boundary: FF4jApiApplicationJersey2x, FF4jAuthenticationFilter, FF4jAuthorizationFilter, FF4jSecurityContext( Holder), ApiConfig, all ff4j-webapi resources and domain beans, ff4j-web servlets/controllers/ConsoleOperations/ConsoleRenderer/FileUtils, plus JDBC/Neo4j/Mongo/Cassandra/Elastic/CouchDB/Redis stores, XmlParser/YamlParser/PropertiesParser, MappingUtil, PropertyFactory and FF4j core. The submitted candidate was traced end-to-end in source (filter → resource → store.clear()).
limitations: No code execution, compilation, deployment or runtime test was performed; all conclusions are source-reading based, and no runtime confirmation is claimed.
Third-party JavaScript/CSS assets under ff4j-web (jQuery, jqPlot, bootstrap, DataTables) and generated/minified resources were only spot-checked, not audited in depth.

Every store backend (HBase, Cassandra, Elastic, CouchDB, GCP, AWS SSM/DynamoDB, Consul, Redis/Lettuce, Ignite, Hazelcast, Neo4j, etc.) was not fully read line-by-line; injections into those backends were sampled via grep.

The presence/absence of container- or application-level additional security (Jersey RolesAllowedDynamicFeature, Spring Security URL rules, servlet filters) in real deployments is unknown from this snapshot and affects the practical exploitability of the submitted candidate.
No repository history, patch or advisory metadata was available (no .git), so it was not possible to confirm which code change introduced the flaw or whether a fix exists upstream.

rejected_leads.lead: Attacker-controlled Java class names passed to Class.forName(...).newInstance()/constructor invocation in the console and API (ConsoleOperations.createFeature/updateFlippingStrategy, FeaturesController.buildFlippingStrategy→MappingUtil.instanceFlippingStrategy, PropertyFactory.createProperty via `pType`/PropertyApiBean.type, FeatureResource upsert via `flippingStrategy.type`, plus XML/YAML/Properties config import).
rejected_leads.reason: Real unsafe-reflection pattern (CWE-470) with several HTTP entry points, but full code-execution impact depends on a suitable gadget class/constructor being present on the classpath and on casts/interfaces restricting what is invoked; reachability also normally requires console/API write access (or an exposed console). It is a strong secondary lead but a lower-confidence, gadget-dependent security impact than the deterministic authorization bypass, so it is not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: Web console edit gating (`adminGroups` → `enableEdit`) is enforced only in Thymeleaf views (AbstractController.makeWebContext lines 219-228; view templates use th:if="${enableEdit}"), while FeaturesController/PropertiesController/HomeController/SettingsController perform enable/disable/delete/create/permission changes without any server-side admin check.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible broken access control (client-side-only enforcement) and state-changing GET operations without CSRF tokens, but the FF4j sample security model expects the console to be protected by the embedding application (e.g. Spring Security + ff4j.consoleAdmin.authenticated), so intent and threat model are ambiguous; left unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: HTML injection/XSS in the deprecated embedded console (ConsoleRenderer renders feature/property ids, descriptions, fixed values and event data into HTML without encoding; notFound() echoes pathInfo).
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker control over stored names exists but impact is confined to the legacy/deprecated `ConsoleServlet` UI and mostly affects an admin session; lower severity and less certain than the API authorization bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded multipart import in HomeController/ConsoleServlet (`new ServletFileUpload(new DiskFileItemFactory()).parseRequest(req)` with no size limits) enabling resource exhaustion.
rejected_leads.reason: Denial-of-service only, requires console access; not the strongest issue.

rejected_leads.lead: Dynamic SQL built by JdbcQueryBuilder.buildWhereClause/buildClauseIn (string concatenation of action/host/name/source filters marked 'FIXME Stop dynamic query').
rejected_leads.reason: Filters in EventQueryDefinition are not populated from HTTP parameters in any reviewed web entry point (only from/to timestamps are), so the concatenated values are not attacker-controlled — rejected as not reachable.

summary: The strongest source-backed issue is a broken authorization enforcement in the FF4j Jersey web API: the read/write role separation advertised by ApiConfig/`@RolesAllowed` is not actually enforced, so a credential that only has the READ role can invoke state-changing/destructive API operations (including clearing the whole feature and property stores). The flaw is rooted in `FF4jAuthorizationFilter`, which only evaluates method-level `@RolesAllowed` annotations (class-level annotations are ignored unless the method also has one) and, when a method-level annotation exists, unions class-level and method-level roles with OR semantics (so `@RolesAllowed(READ)` at class level satisfies a method-level `@RolesAllowed(WRITE)`). Destructive endpoints such as `FeatureStoreResource.clearFeatures()`/`createSchema()` and `PropertyStoreResource.clearProperties()`/`createSchema()` carry no method-level `@RolesAllowed(WRITE)`, and `GroupResource` enable/disable carry WRITE only as a method annotation while the class declares READ.
